paras: The Franklin County whitecapper arrests took place in February 1903 in Franklin County, Mississippi, when white neighbors of a Black farmer warned in writing to leave the county lay in wait at his house and captured eight members of a mounted band. The eight were bound over at $2,000 each for intimidating Black residents to make them leave, and days later the circuit judge and district attorney announced a wider campaign of arrests. Mississippi papers praised the capture, one editor calling it proof that "the white southern man is the best friend the negro has."

In early 1903 white papers described Franklin County and neighboring Lincoln and Amite counties as a center of "whitecapping," in which bands of night riders drove Black residents away. Circuit Judge Jeff Truly was said to have had most of the recent whitecapping cases in his district.

The farmer was not named in any report; one dispatch described him as "a well-to-do and respected negro farmer." He received a written warning to leave the county and told white neighbors, who, according to the Hattiesburg Daily Progress, advised him to stay so they could "catch the whitecappers redhanded." About midnight, according to a special from Knoxville dated February 9, a body of horsemen rode up to his cabin, and the waiting posse surrounded them and captured eight.

Accounts of the trap differ: the Knoxville special said a posse guarded his home, the Port Gibson Reveille and the Hattiesburg paper said white men hid inside the house, and another Vicksburg dispatch said a posse "took them in the rear." The special placed the capture on the previous night, while the Reveille said only "a few nights ago." No report describes any injury to the farmer.

The Knoxville special said the eight were bound over to the criminal court in bonds of $2,000 each, while the Water Valley Progress named a magistrate's court and the Hattiesburg paper said the farmer had made affidavits against them. The charge was intimidating negroes "for the purpose of causing them to leave the county," which the Water Valley paper rendered as "intimidating negroes and driving off labor."

On February 13 a Vicksburg dispatch reported that Judge Truly and District Attorney Ratcliffe had begun "a vigorous campaign" against Franklin County whitecappers, with thirteen arrests and warrants for twenty-two others, said to include several prominent men. In April the Franklin County grand jury at Meadville indicted twelve persons for whitecapping, with trial put off to the next term. The report did not say whether the eight were among them, and no report of a trial was found.

The Knoxville special ran on February 10 in the Montgomery Advertiser, in fragmentary form in the Indianapolis Journal, and in the Birmingham Age-Herald, whose subhead, "White Men Arrested In Mississippi for Issuing Warnings," named a race the dispatch did not. A second version, headed "Whitecappers Caught," ran in the Waxahachie Daily Light and the Shreveport Caucasian, calling the accused "alleged white-cappers" and "regulators." The arrest campaign was reported in Alabama, Louisiana and Texas papers on February 14 and 15, the Montgomery Advertiser heading it "War on Whitecappers."

Mississippi papers framed the capture as white citizens acting against lawlessness on a Black neighbor's behalf. The Port Gibson Reveille said the whitecappers "were very much suprised" and printed the item beside a reprinted Starkville Farm Gazette editorial blaming race agitation for whitecapping and lost farm labor. The Hattiesburg Daily Progress called it "the best thing that has happened in a long time" and invited the northern press to take it as evidence of white southern friendship for Black people.
No Black-press account of the incident was found; all located coverage comes from white papers.

reader.title: Franklin County whitecapper arrests
bases: A band of night riders called whitecappers rode to a Black farmer's house to drive him from the county after a written warning, and were charged with intimidating negroes to make them leave (A5, A7, A10).

The Vicksburg specials (A5, A4) and separately worded Mississippi accounts (A7, A9, A10) agree that a warned Black man's white neighbors trapped a band at his house and that eight were held under $2,000 bonds, though they differ on details of the trap.

accounts.label: Vicksburg special from Knoxville (Feb. 9)
accounts.gist: A negro warned in writing to leave told the whites; a posse guarded his home, and about midnight surrounded and captured eight of a body of horsemen, who were bound over at $2,000 each.

accounts.label: Vicksburg 'Whitecappers Caught' version (Feb. 10-11)
accounts.gist: White neighbors told a respected negro farmer to stay; when the regulators surrounded his house the following night a posse took them in the rear and captured eight, who were jailed at Knoxville.

accounts.label: Mississippi local briefs and editorial
accounts.gist: White men hidden in the house stepped out and recognized eight whitecappers, who were arrested next day; the farmer made affidavits against them.

info: Night of about February 8, 1903 ('last night' in a Vicksburg special dated Feb. 9); other accounts say 'a few nights ago' or 'the following night' after the notice
A Black farmer's house (cabin) in Franklin County; the special came from Knoxville, the county seat, where the eight were jailed; the exact location of the house is not given
One unnamed Black man, described as 'a well-to-do and respected negro farmer' and as a negro 'who had always borne a good reputation'; not harmed
None against the farmer; no reason for the warning is reported
